findings.where: First screen, Mark's photograph and the slate ground (desktop and phone); also the 'Graded for the site' texture specimen and the motion-sketch thumbnail
findings.fault: The photo isn't graded into the house blue-grey. Its backdrop is keyed out to flat slate, so Mark is a cut-out head and shoulders pasted onto a flat navy field, not a full-bleed photograph of a man speaking in a room. The skin and the red tie keep their own colour, and nothing in the frame keeps the photo's light or depth. At hero scale the cut edge around the hair shows. In the texture specimen the key has eaten a slate wedge out of the blue lectern sign at the bottom right. The page says this same key will be applied to every new photograph, so the problem belongs to the method, not just to this stand-in.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first and asked for 'real people in real light' and a photograph graded into the house colours. A cut-out on a flat colour field looks like a cheap composite, close to the 'slick' and 'cheesy' the brief rules out. A development-bank visitor sees a pasted portrait, not an advisor at work.

findings.where: Article specimen, the numbered list's numerals (1., 2., 3.); the palette's blue entry, which assigns 'list numbers' to blue
findings.fault: The list numerals are in the house blue but can't be clicked. The page's own colour rule, stated in the specimen note, is 'blue only where something can be clicked', and on this page blue otherwise marks links, the PDF download and the action. The numerals give the blue a second, decorative job and break the one signal the palette is built on.
findings.who_objects: A reader of Mark's articles, who learns from the rest of the page that blue means a link and may try the numerals or start doubting the cue. Angélique, adding lists to new articles, inherits a colour rule that contradicts itself.
